extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalists, political leaders, and anyone studying public opinion and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how diverse private impressions and motives are converted into a common will or public opinion, and the techniques and psychological principles by which leaders and communicators induce collective agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: The materialistic conception that economic position determines opinion is inadequate: a man's many economic relations may incline him in different directions and it is rarely obvious which relation is producing a particular opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single economic relation explains an individual's view; special inquiry is needed to identify which contact or relation is relevant. Economic position predicts tendencies (e.g., owners resist deprivation) but cannot prophesy detailed views or choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class interest is not fixed or singular
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fixed set of opinions tied to a class; class interest can be conceived narrowly or broadly, selfishly or unselfishly, and may be based on varying facts, truths, or errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating 'class interest' as a single coherent policy program. Even under communal ownership, divergent conceptions of interest will create new class-like divisions unless people see the system in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of deterministic social prediction (Marx/Lenin lesson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to deduce a people's actions solely from their economic interests lead to wrong predictions; historical events (e.g., socialist revolutions not following Marx's timetable) show that clear conceptions of interest do not automatically arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of grand predictive schemes that rely on assumed uniform political consciousness derived from economic conditions; empirical testing and attention to contingent factors are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinct and disposition are conditioned by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate dispositions (instincts) do not rigidly produce fixed social behavior; experience, memory, and learning determine what will excite an instinct and the means by which it is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining behavior, account for the cognitive and affective modification of instincts by culture and experience rather than assuming blind innate drives determine social action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability of stimulus-response attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions and appetites are attachable to many different objects and gratifications; the specific stimulus that arouses a response is casual and culturally variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that similar emotional responses can be triggered by different objects across times and places; explanations must allow for cultural and historical variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion is transferable via conditioned response
rubrics_metrics.description: An emotion originally attached to one idea or object can become associated with other ideas, names, or symbols through substitution and conditioning, allowing leaders to redirect feeling from complex realities to simpler symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To mobilize diverse groups, identify substitute stimuli or symbols that evoke the same emotion across them; to analyze campaigns, trace how emotional attachments were transferred from original facts to symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols (binders) as tools of coalition-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Americanism', 'Lincoln', 'Progressivism' function as symbolic 'binders' that mean different things to different people but unite them by containing their emotions and preventing scrutiny of specific programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders who capture and control current symbols control the situation; political messaging often intentionally uses ambiguous symbolic language to form coalitions from heterogeneous opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical vagueness and obscurantism unite heterogeneous opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vagueness at crucial points in public debate is a common technique when a leader seeks superficial harmony among conflicting factions; obscurantism often signals cross-purposes rather than clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert that deliberate ambiguity (stretching words to mean 'all things to all men', choosing non-explosive subjects) is a tactic to prevent divisions from surfacing; such vagueness reduces critical scrutiny of measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader's technic for securing a homogeneous vote
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a majority out of divergent opinions, a leader selects safe opening subjects, uses binders and evocative names, stretches meanings of contested terms, emphasizes non-controversial details, and balances themes to placate opposing factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In campaign messaging: (a) avoid or neutralize explosive issues, (b) invoke respected names/symbols to transfer piety or loyalty, (c) employ formulas that cover opposed aims (e.g., 'American rights'), and (d) combine themes to give different audiences something they can read into the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation by cancellation produces the 'least common denominator' decision
rubrics_metrics.description: When many conflicting motives and reasons are aggregated (e.g., in an election), contradictions often cancel each other, leaving a simple least common denominator (such as desire for change) that determines outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting aggregate choices (like vote totals) requires care: counts do not reveal the underlying distribution of motives without further inquiry; policy-makers must recognize that the public opinion they face may differ from the motives that elected them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern communications enable engineered common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: New media (cable, radio, telegraph, daily press) make it possible to present the same names and ideas simultaneously to many peoples, enabling attempts (e.g., the Fourteen Points) to knit a common consciousness across diverse audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicators can exploit mass media to synchronize symbols and messages, but must attend to the underlying temper and circumstances that make audiences receptive; timing and context (war weariness, demoralization) matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and fragility of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols have limits: overuse, violent abuse of the realities they purport to represent, or severe contrary events can 'burst' a symbol (e.g., Holy Russia collapsing under suffering and defeat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain symbol credibility by aligning symbols with realities and avoiding gross contradictions; be aware that dramatic events can abruptly destroy a symbol's unifying power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect cognition and action in mass affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: In mass politics individuals often possess only dim, second-hand ideas of distant events and satisfy emotions through indirect means (donating to organizations, voting for parties) rather than acting directly upon the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should distinguish between first-hand emotional experience and the indirect cognitive bases for political acts; strategies that appeal to feeling can be effective even when factual knowledge is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: You cannot infer individual motives from aggregate actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting votes or observing mass actions does not reveal what moved each person: many voters support the same ticket for very different and sometimes contradictory reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic inferences about motives from electoral results; use special inquiry (surveys, interviews, qualitative research) to uncover the varied motives behind collective behavior.
